title: Why You Shouldn't Respond When A Difficult Student Has A Good Day student-has-a-good-day/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues, counterintuitively, that the best response to a difficult student's good day is often no special response at all. He explains that rewarding good behavior with prizes or effusive praise externalizes motivation and teaches students that positive behavior is something they should be paid for rather than a reward in itself. Instead, treating the student normally—like every other student—lets the good behavior remain intrinsically satisfying and helps dissolve the labels the student has carried. The piece frames this restraint as ultimately more empowering and respectful than celebration, since it communicates that the student's dignity was never conditional on being 'special' or 'fixed.'
points: Rewarding a difficult student's good day with prizes or effusive praise externalizes their motivation and cheapens the achievement.
Good behavior should be treated as its own reward, since intrinsic motivation is necessary for lasting behavioral change.
Treating the student like everyone else after a good day, rather than singling them out, restores their sense of being a regular class member.
Excessive celebration of good behavior can paradoxically signal the student is still viewed as an exception or outcast.
The article recommends only subtle, wordless acknowledgment—like a handshake days later—rather than immediate praise.
quotes: When a difficult student has a good day it’s normal to want to reward them for it.
But the truth is, the best response you can offer a difficult student after a good day is no response at all.
When you reward students for good behavior they become externally motivated.
Real and lasting change only happens when difficult students are intrinsically motivated to behave.
That isn’t to say that you should shun or ignore difficult students after a good day. You’ll just treat them like everyone else.
But how do you describe the view from the summit of Mount Everest?
